Identity confirmed at lines 101-103 ('E-Cun (Buyang)' as representative va…
new_statements.rule_in_words: E'ma (Ecun) Buyang is a six-tone language; no accessible source states where word stress falls. The only prominence-related statements in the Buyang literature concern the sesquisyllabic word shape: prefixal presyllables (qa-, ma-, ta-, ka-, pa-) are toneless / neutral-tone (Chinese sources: 轻声, 'lightly read') before a full tone-bearing root syllable, i.e. weak-initial + strong-final disyllables; this is stated first-hand for Paha (Li & Luo 2006/2010), for 'Buyang' generally in Li 1998's abstract, and second-hand (from Li 1999, Langjia data) by Edmondson. None of these is an explicit stress rule and none is specifically about the E'ma variety.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Li & Luo 2010:11 (Paha): some prefixes alternate between a full phonemic tone and the neutral tone (pa33 ~ pa0); Li 1998 abstract: prefixes read mid-level 33 in slow speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prefix + root disyllables, citation forms); Paha tone sandhi in polysyllables described as not yet generalisable. The Ostapirat quote is E'ma-specific but tone-only; the neutral-tone-prefix quote is from the sibling language Baha Buyang (baha1256).
new_statements.identity_note: E'ma Buyang (yzg, emab1235) = the Ecun-group villages (Ecun, Dugan, Zhelong, Nada, Longna, Maguan) of Gula township, Funing; Li & Luo 2006/2010 explicitly say E'ma is 'represented by Ecun'. The open first-hand descriptions downloaded (PL-607, LTBA 29.1) describe PAHA = Baha Buyang (baha1256, yha, Yanglian village, Guangnan), a different ISO language; Edmondson's and Sagart's Buyang data are Langjia = Langnian Buyang (yln). Ostapirat 2000's 'Buyang (n)' data ARE from E-Cun (his own fieldwork) but give tones only. So the neutral-tone-prefix statement quoted is sibling-variety evidence, not an E'ma statement.

tone_statements.quote: Buyang possesses six tones: /24/, /44/, /45/, /53/, /42/, and /213/. Tone /42/ is accompanied by a glottal closure at the end, while tone /213/ is accompanied by creakiness, which starts in the middle of the pitch and continues through its rising part. Two tones, /45/ and /53/, may occur with checked syllables. … The glottalized initials only occur with series 1 tones (i.e. tones /24/, /45/, and /42/). Other initials may occur with any of the six tones.

tone_statements.summary: Six tones in E-Cun Buyang: 24, 44, 45, 53, 42 (with final glottal closure) and 213 (creaky); only 45 and 53 occur on checked syllables. Author's own field data. Nothing on word stress.

tone_statements.quote: The Buyang languages are spoken in eight villages of Gula township, Wenshan prefecture, Yunnan. Among these, the speech used at the Langjia location is considered by the Buyang speakers to be most different from the others. Yet, linguistically speaking, the Langjia dialect is still very close to those at the other locations, with differences between them falling mainly in their modern tonal reflexes. Material on the representative variety in this study is collected from the E-Cun location. ... [p. 238:] The tones are indicated according to their proto-tone categories by the letters *A, *B, *C and *D
tone_statements.locator: sec. 5.4 'Buyang Varieties', p. 257; tone notation sec. 2, p. 238; E-Cun tonal reflexes in Tables 20, 21, 21a, pp. 258-259
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone; E-Cun reflexes by proto-tone class in the tables: *A1 > 24 (rising), *A2 > 44 (level), *C1 > 42, *C2 > 213, *D1 (long) > 45, *D2 (long) > 53, i.e. the six tones /24 44 45 53 42 213/ of the author's Proto-Kra description; checked syllables take 45/53; TBU, sandhi and stress not discussed here.
